title: A Personalised mRNA Vaccine Just Halved Melanoma Recurrence Over Five Years. Cancer Treatment May Never Be the Same.
excerpt: Moderna and Merck's KEYNOTE-942 trial shows the vaccine kept 92 per cent of patients alive at the five-year mark, compared with 71 per cent on standard immunotherapy alone. South Asians, often diagnosed later, have the most to gain from a treatment that learns each tumour's fingerprint.
body:
The same mRNA technology that produced COVID-19 vaccines in record time is now showing it can keep cancer from coming back — for at least five years.

At the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting in Chicago, Moderna and Merck presented five-year follow-up data from the Phase 2b KEYNOTE-942 trial. The results were striking: a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine called intismeran autogene, given alongside Merck's immunotherapy drug Keytruda, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 49 per cent compared with Keytruda alone. The risk of the cancer spreading to distant organs dropped by 59 per cent.

The overall survival numbers are even more telling. After five years, 92.2 per cent of patients who received the combination therapy were still alive. In the Keytruda-only group, that figure was 71.3 per cent. The results were published simultaneously in the *Journal of Clinical Oncology*.

## How the Vaccine Works

Unlike traditional vaccines that prevent infection, intismeran autogene is a therapeutic vaccine — given after surgery to stop cancer from returning. Each dose is custom-built from the patient's own tumour. Researchers sequence the tumour's DNA, identify mutations unique to those cancer cells, and encode up to 34 of those mutations into a single mRNA molecule. When injected, the vaccine teaches the immune system to recognise and destroy any cells carrying those specific alterations.

"The vaccine can be considered a personalised approach that is tumour-informed," said Dr Janice Mehnert, a professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and the study's senior investigator. "This is given with anti-PD-1 therapy to result in truly personalised treatment."

The trial enrolled 157 patients with high-risk stage III and IV melanoma whose tumours had been surgically removed. Of these, 107 received the vaccine-Keytruda combination, while 50 received Keytruda alone.

## Why This Matters for South Asian Families

Melanoma has long been considered a disease of lighter-skinned populations, and that assumption has real consequences for the diaspora. South Asians are often diagnosed at later stages because neither patients nor doctors are looking for it. A 2022 study in the *Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology* found that people with darker skin tones were significantly more likely to be diagnosed with advanced-stage melanoma and had worse outcomes.

A treatment that works after surgery — one that can prevent the cancer from spreading even when caught late — is particularly relevant for populations where early detection remains uneven.

There is also a broader significance. If personalised mRNA vaccines prove effective in larger trials, they could reshape treatment for multiple cancers. Moderna and Merck currently have nine Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials running across different tumour types, including non-small cell lung cancer, kidney cancer, and bladder cancer.

## The Manufacturing Challenge

Personalised medicine comes with a personalised price tag. Each vaccine dose must be manufactured individually, starting from a biopsy of the patient's tumour. The turnaround time and cost remain significant hurdles. Dr Mehnert acknowledged that "the vaccine does take time to make," though she noted that manufacturing capacity has expanded substantially since the trial began.

Presenting author Dr Matteo Carlino of the Melanoma Institute Australia added that "many thousands of patients have received intismeran on multiple clinical trials, and capacity is now in place."

## What Comes Next

The Phase 3 confirmatory trial is already underway. If it replicates these results, personalised mRNA cancer vaccines could become part of standard treatment within the next few years.

For Indian families in the United States, the takeaway is twofold. First, melanoma screening matters regardless of skin tone — ask your dermatologist about it at your next visit. Second, the same mRNA platform that delivered pandemic vaccines at unprecedented speed is now being turned against cancer with results that, five years in, are holding up.

The technology is not a cure. But it is the strongest evidence yet that the immune system, properly trained, can keep cancer from returning for years.

*Sources: ASCO 2026 Annual Meeting; Journal of Clinical Oncology (June 2026); Merck/Moderna press release (June 1, 2026); Medical News Today; Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology*
